title: Finite-time Scaling of the surface special transition in a 3D classical Heisenberg model
authors: Dongxu Liu, Zhe Wang, Shuai Yin, Zheng Yan
abstract: We investigate nonequilibrium driven dynamics across the special surface phase transition in the three-dimensional classical Heisenberg model with open boundaries, where tuning the surface coupling gives access to an extraordinary-log boundary critical state characterized by logarithmic, rather than power-law, decay of correlations. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we realize four driving protocols: temperature heating and cooling across the special transition, and surface-coupling ramps from the ordinary and extraordinary-log critical states into the special point. For temperature-driven protocols, the surface order parameter obeys a generalization of the finite-time scaling (FTS) and the Kibble-Zurek mechanism. The central finding emerges when the system is driven from the extraordinary-log critical state: the large-rate scaling relation acquires a logarithmic correction and takes the novel form $M^{2}_{s}\propto R^{(1+η_{s})/r_{s}}[\log(LR^{1/η_{s}})]^{-q}$ , where $R$ is the driving rate, $L$ the system size, $η_{s}$ the surface anomalous dimension, $r_{s}$ the scaling dimension of $R$, and $q$ the exponent governing the logarithmic boundary criticality. We demonstrate that this form follows from the general FTS framework by incorporating the logarithmic initial-state memory, and we achieve excellent data collapse over a wide range of system sizes and driving rates. Our results establish that extraordinary-log initial states alter nonequilibrium critical scaling, extending boundary FTS beyond conventional power-law initial conditions.
summary: This paper investigates how a 3D classical Heisenberg model behaves when driven across a surface phase transition. The authors find that the initial critical state dictates the resulting non-equilibrium scaling laws. Specifically, starting from an extraordinary-log critical point introduces a novel logarithmic correction to the standard finite-time scaling predictions.
main_problem: The study investigates non-equilibrium driven dynamics across a surface special phase transition in a 3D classical Heisenberg model, focusing on how the initial critical state influences scaling laws.
main_result: When driven from an extraordinary-log critical state, the finite-time scaling relation acquires a novel logarithmic correction: $M^2_{s} \propto R^{(1+\eta_s)/r_s}[\log(LR/r_s)]^{-q}$.
method: The research employs Monte Carlo simulations to test four different driving protocols (temperature and surface-coupling ramps) across the transition point.
model_or_system: The system is a three-dimensional classical Heisenberg model with open boundaries, described by an interaction Hamiltonian involving bulk and surface couplings.
key_observables: Surface order parameter mean squared ($\langle M^2_s angle$), which is analyzed for its scaling behavior with the driving rate ($R$).
important_parameters: The analysis distinguishes between ordinary, special, and extraordinary-log critical states; key parameters include the driving rate $R$, system size $L$, and various anomalous dimensions ($\eta_s, r_s$).
main_assumptions: The work extends Finite-Time Scaling (FTS) theory by incorporating 'logarithmic initial-state memory' into the general scaling framework.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the driven dynamics of $M^2_s$ for non-equilibrium heating and cooling, showing power-law scaling; other figures demonstrate data collapse across different quench protocols.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes temperature-driven and surface-coupling ramped protocols. It first establishes standard Finite-Time Scaling (FTS) behavior for certain drives, then presents the central finding regarding the modified scaling law when starting from an extraordinary-log critical state.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the study of non-equilibrium dynamics and memory effects in critical systems provides foundational concepts applicable to understanding quench dynamics in quantum many-body systems or open quantum systems far from equilibrium.
